JSON: Name: retinal_fixation_target_optimization Title: Retinal eye-tracking assessment of fixation-target design to minimize fixational eye movements during sustained fixation Short Hypothesis: Fixation targets that include a small, high-contrast central feature cause a reduction in the spatial spread of gaze and in the magnitude of microsaccade and drift displacements during sustained fixation, compared with fixation targets lacking a small central feature, when measured with a high-precision retinal eye tracker. Related Work: Prior work on fixation-target design produced inconsistent results: some behavioral studies using video-based eye trackers reported small or no effects of target contrast, color, or background on overall fixation stability, while other studies reported that smaller or sharper central features reduce gaze dispersion or increase microsaccade incidence. A small number of high-precision studies and one study using a retinal tracker suggested that targets with a small central feature or multiple high-contrast components can reduce gaze spread, but these studies either focused on different tasks (active discrimination vs passive fixation) or had limited sample sizes. Major limitations across existing approaches include reliance on video-based trackers that lack the precision to resolve microsaccades and drift reliably and that are vulnerable to pupil-size artifacts and small head movements, inconsistent operational definitions of stability (BCEA, microsaccade rate, drift metrics), and sparse direct comparisons between target geometries, polarities, and measurement technologies. Dynamic fixation stimuli have been minimally explored with respect to fixational movement properties. Abstract: This study evaluates how fixation-target design influences microsaccades and ocular drift during sustained fixation using a high-precision retinal eye tracker. We compare five canonical static target geometries differing in central feature presence (small point, cross, smooth Bessel, Gaussian blob, and simple circle) across two polarity conditions (white-on-black, black-on-grey). Using within-subject repeated measures, we quantify overall gaze dispersion and separate microsaccade and drift properties (rate, displacement, path length, speed, and direction). We additionally benchmark measurements against a high-end video-based eye tracker to quantify measurement artifacts. The main contribution is a rigorously controlled, measurement-informed pipeline that isolates how small central features and display polarity causally affect fixational eye movements. Expected outcomes are (1) demonstration that small central features reduce gaze spread and movement magnitudes when measured with a retinal tracker, and (2) quantification of biases introduced by video-based tracking. Results will inform methodological choices for experiments and clinical procedures requiring minimized fixation variability. Experiments: Participants: N = 24 adult participants with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, within-subject design. Stimuli: Five static fixation targets: (1) Gaussian blob, (2) simple Circle, (3) small Point, (4) Circle-Cross-Point (CCP), (5) Bessel-function ring; rendered in two polarity conditions: white-on-black and black-on-grey. Measurement hardware: Primary recorder = retinal eye tracker (FreezEyeTracker or equivalent; sampling >= 600 Hz; RMS sample-to-sample noise <= 0.2 deg). Baseline recorder = high-end video-based eye tracker (e.g., Tobii Pro Spectrum; sampling >= 600 Hz where possible; RMS sample-to-sample noise ~2.4 deg). Procedure: Each participant performs 2 (polarity) x 5 (targets) repeated blocks. Each block: 30 s sustained fixation on a single target; 3 s randomized mask between blocks; at least 4 sessions per polarity per participant, randomized order. Preprocessing: blink detection and removal; split recordings by target and session; compute gaze zero-point using short-center fixation episodes before main blocks; reject saccades/drift events >2.5 deg from target center. Event detection: microsaccades detected with Engbert & Kliegl algorithm, λ = 6, minimum duration threshold per original algorithm, minimum amplitude threshold = 0.067 deg (4 arcmin); merge saccades separated <20 ms. Drift episodes defined as inter-saccadic intervals >100 ms without data loss. Metrics: overall BCEA (68.27% ellipse), microsaccade rate (Hz), microsaccade displacement (deg), microsaccade direction distribution, drift displacement (deg), drift path length (deg), drift speed (deg/s), SWJ incidence. Statistical analysis: Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA (2 polarity x 5 target) with participant random effects; report Bayes factors and 95% credible intervals; complementary frequentist repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction and effect sizes (partial η2). Pairwise comparisons: Bayesian t-tests with directional hypotheses; control family-wise error where applicable. Comparisons/ablations: (A) Ablation 1: remove small central feature (compare CCP vs Circle) to isolate central-feature effect. (B) Ablation 2: vary central-feature size in three levels to estimate dose-response on microsaccade rate and displacement. (C) Measurement baseline: concurrent recording with video-based tracker to compute differences in BCEA and event-level metrics and to estimate pupil-size artifact influence. Power and sample size: sample size chosen to detect within-subject medium effect (dz = 0.6) at 95% power and alpha = 0.05. Data reporting: per-participant distributions, group-level Bayes factors, effect sizes, and full event lists for microsaccades and drift episodes. Pre-registration: record hypotheses, analysis pipeline, and exclusion rules prior to data collection. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical dependence on availability and stability of retinal eye-tracker hardware; prototype devices may fail or produce variable RMS noise across sessions. Measurement baseline comparison is confounded by different measurement principles; alignment and synchronization between retinal and video-based systems may introduce timing or spatial registration errors. Microsaccade detection thresholds and parameter choices (λ, duration, amplitude) can affect event counts and estimated rates, producing analysis sensitivity. Participant variability: individual differences in microsaccade directionality and SWJ incidence may inflate within-subject variance and reduce reproducibility. Small effect sizes: differences between targets may be near measurement noise floor for some metrics, requiring larger samples. Generalization limits: results from healthy adults may not transfer to clinical populations or to tasks with active visual demands. Display geometry and peripheral cues (screen edges, background borders) can interact with target polarity, introducing uncontrolled stabilization cues. Computational limits: high-sample-rate retinal data increases storage and processing time and may require optimized pipelines. Evaluation bias: reliance on BCEA and event-level summaries may obscure temporally localized effects or nonlinear dependencies between microsaccades and drift.
